newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: IMF tells Czechs to go slow on lowering rates.
newsitem.headline: IMF tells Czechs to go slow on lowering rates.

text.p: A mission of the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday that it had stressed to Czech officials to be careful in lowering interest rates so as not to cause a further weakening of the Czech crown.

"(The mission) stressed... the necessity for a careful approach to lowering interest rates so that there would not be an undesirable weakening of the crown exchange rate," IMF Czech representative Jiri Jonas said in a statement.

It said that a meeting between the IMF delegation, Czech National Bank Governor Josef Tosovsky and representatives of the finance ministry on Thursday agreed to continue a dialogue to evaluate restrictive fiscal steps taken, and to formulate further necessary steps to correct imbalances in the economy.
"The mission supported the announced (state) budget cuts as measures heading in the right direction," it said.

After the Czech National Bank was forced to float the crown on May 27, the government announced a package of spending cuts to reduce domestic demand which when added to an April round of spending cuts totalled 45.5 billion crowns.
The cuts were needed, economists say, to slow down a ballooning trade deficit which had weakened investor interest in the Czech crown.
The IMF mission gave no further details on its analysis of the Czech crown or interest lates.
The Czech National Bank, facing attacks on the currency in May, sharply raised rates -- especially short-term rates -- to cut off funds for specualtive short-selling of the crown.

The central bank, with commercial banks and industry clamouring for more liquidity, agreed this week to lift restrictions on non-resident participation in the money market and has gradually lowered rates on its open market operations.

The central bank's repo rate has come down to 25 percent from 75 percent at the height of the crown crisis. Many analysts expect a lowering soon of the last resort Lombard facility from its current 50 percent level.
The bank's key discount rate was raised to 13 percent from 10.5 percent after the crown was floated.
Many analysts think that the currency can still weaken significantly when rates relax and liqiuidty returns.
The Prague investment house WoodCommerz said on Thursday that it expected the crown to still fall to 34-35 to the dollar by the year's end from current levels around 32.

The special IMF mission -- which over the past week has met with senior government, central bank, and labour union officials and ended on Thursday -- said that it rejected suggestions that import surcharges and other administrative restrictions be installed to help the trade balance.
"The mission rejected the resolution of external imbalances through import surcharges and further administrative measures as unrealistic and damaging," it said without elaborating.
